prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: This, Filling, Blue

outputs.L1:
This is where you leave me. Filling of old salt and ponderous,  
what’s left of your voice in the air. Blue honeycreeper thrashed out  
to a ragged wind, whole months  
spent crawling this white beach,  
raked like a thumb, shucking, swallowing  
the sea’s benediction, pearled oxides.

Out here, I am the body invented naked,  
woman emerging from cold seas, herself  
the raw eel-froth met beneath her tangles,  
who must believe with all her puckering  
holes. What wounds the Poinciana slits  
forth, what must turn red eventually.  
The talon-mouths undressing. The cling-cling  
bird scratching its one message; the arm  
you broke, reset, and broke again. Caribbean.

Sky, a wound I am licking until I am drawn new  
as a lamb, helpless in the chicken wire of my sex.  
I let every stranger in. Watch men change faces  
with the run-down sun, count fires  
in the loom-holes of their pickups, lines of rot,  
studying their scarred window-plagues,  
nightshade my own throat closed tight  
against a hard hand. Then all comes mute  
in my glittering eye. All is knocked back:  
slick hem-suck of the dark surf, ceramic  
tiles approaching, the blur of a beard.  
The white tusk of his ocean goring me.  
This world, unforgiving in its boundaries.  
The day’s owl and its omen  
slipping a bright hook  
into my cheek—
outputs.L2:
Here is the place where you abandon me,  
saturated with ancient salt and heaviness,  
while the last trace of your voice hovers nearby.  
A blue honeycreeper struggles against  
a fraying wind. Entire months pass  
as I drag myself along this pale shore,  
combed smooth as if by a thumb, opening shells  
and drinking the sea’s blessing, its lustrous rusts.

Beyond everything, I become a body imagined without clothes:  
a woman rising out of freezing water,  
herself the crude foam of eels caught in her snarled hair,  
forced to trust through every tightened opening.  
The Poinciana releases whatever injures it,  
and whatever emerges must finally redden.  
Clawed mouths strip things bare. The cling-cling bird  
scrapes out its single warning; the arm  
you fractured was set, then fractured once more. The Caribbean.

The heavens are an injury beneath my tongue  
until I am remade like a newborn lamb,  
powerless inside the wire cage of my womanhood.  
I admit every unknown man. I watch their features alter  
as the exhausted sun descends, tally the flames  
glowing through the woven gaps of their trucks, the seams of decay,  
and inspect their windows, scarred like afflictions.  
Like nightshade, I seal my throat  
against the pressure of a brutal hand.

Then everything falls silent  
inside my sparkling eye. Everything recoils:  
the dark tide’s wet pull at the hem,  
ceramic squares drawing closer,  
a beard dissolving into haze.  
His ocean’s ivory fang pierces me.  
This world shows no mercy at its borders.  
The daylight owl and its prophecy  
slide a shining barb into my face—
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker who has been abandoned and is left alone with the lingering memory of another person’s voice. Although the relationship itself has ended, that voice continues to haunt her, making the past feel painfully present. Her emotional state is reflected in the Caribbean landscape, which becomes more than a backdrop: its exposed, damaged, and unstable features mirror her wounds, vulnerability, and difficult effort to reconstruct her identity.

Throughout the poem, images of brokenness, blood, and predatory birds suggest that the speaker’s suffering is both physical and emotional. These recurring images create a sense of trauma that is not confined to a single event but repeatedly returns. In response to her loneliness, the speaker seeks intimacy with strangers, perhaps hoping that temporary connection will help her recover what she has lost. Yet these encounters offer no real security, as desire remains closely linked to violence, danger, and fear.

By the end of the poem, the world appears harsh and unforgiving. The speaker’s attempts to remake herself have not freed her from pain; instead, threatening and ominous forces pierce her once again. The ending therefore emphasizes the persistence of trauma, suggesting that abandonment has left her exposed to a cycle of longing, vulnerability, and renewed injury.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores abandonment, trauma, sexuality, and vulnerability within a Caribbean setting, using visceral bodily imagery and a landscape marked by beauty as well as danger. Coastlines, birds, wounds, and fragments of violent memory recur throughout the poem, blurring the boundaries between the speaker’s body and the natural world. The sea and shore do not function merely as background; they become active forces that carry traces of loss, exposure, and instability. Likewise, images of injured flesh and vulnerable creatures suggest that personal suffering belongs to a broader environment shaped by predation and historical violence.

The poem’s fragmented structure reflects the speaker’s experience of trauma. Memories appear in flashes rather than as a continuous narrative, conveying how violence disrupts time, identity, and language. Sexuality is presented as a source of intimacy and self-knowledge, but also as a condition that can leave the speaker exposed to judgment, abandonment, or harm. Desire therefore remains inseparable from fear. The body becomes both the site where violence is endured and the means through which the speaker attempts to reclaim a sense of self.

Throughout the poem, the speaker is repeatedly broken apart and remade. This process suggests resilience, but it does not offer a simple story of healing or triumph. Each act of reinvention takes place under threatening conditions, and survival never guarantees safety. Although the speaker continues to adapt, the wounds of the past remain present, while the surrounding world offers little protection. Ultimately, the poem portrays survival as an ongoing and incomplete struggle: the self can be reconstructed after abandonment and violence, but it remains vulnerable to forces that are larger, harsher, and profoundly unforgiving.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, visceral free-verse poem about abandonment, sexual vulnerability, and violence on a Caribbean beach, using dense natural imagery and fragmented syntax.
counterfactuals.output:
At low tide you left me  
where the reef bares its black teeth—  
parrotfish dust, conch-blood,  
a necklace of flies tightening  
around the day.

My dress—salt-stiffened hibiscus—  
open at the throat.  
Every button a small moon  
torn from its orbit.

I had said stay  
but the sea chewed the word to foam,  
white spit sliding back  
between the mangrove’s knuckled roots.

No witness.

Only pelicans dropping like knives,  
only palms with their green applause,  
only the sun—  
that yellow wound—  
pressing its thumb into my shoulder.

Your absence grew hands.

It entered me without entering:  
the shadow of a blade,  
the memory of your mouth  
gone metallic,  
gone stranger.

Across the sand, broken bottles  
flowered blue and murderous.  
A crab lifted one red claw  
as if swearing an oath  
to no god I knew.

Then men—or weather—  
came down the beach.

Footsteps.  
Rum.  
A radio coughing brass.  
The obscene sweetness of guava  
split underfoot.

I became animal-small:  
knees to ribs, breath buried,  
skin a country without borders.  
Their laughter struck the water  
and returned sharpened.

What happened—  
or almost—  
lives under my tongue:

a rusted coin,  
a fishhook,  
a door with no house.

Night arrived in bruises.  
Jellyfish lanterns pulsed offshore.  
The moon dragged its pale machete  
through the clouds.

Still the Caribbean glittered—  
indifferent cathedral,  
blue altar heaped with teeth.

I washed myself in it.

Salt entered every hidden tear,  
every place where tenderness  
had mistaken itself for shelter.

Behind me, the beach erased  
the struggle grain by grain.

Ahead—nothing  
but water,  
water,  
water wearing your face

and refusing  
to drown.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary lyric poem in the voice of a woman left alone by the sea. Include tropical birds, Poinciana, salt, surf, pickup trucks, bodily wounds, and an ominous final image involving a fishhook.
counterfactuals.output:
**After You Drove Inland**

The morning opens its blue mouth  
and says nothing of you.

Only the green parrots riot  
in the Poinciana, shaking loose  
red blossoms like small alarms.  
I sweep them from the porch, barefoot,  
salt whitening my ankles,  
your last tire tracks already softened  
by wind.

Pickup trucks growl along the coast road,  
beds crowded with nets, coolers, men  
who lift two fingers as they pass.  
They know I am the woman  
whose door keeps swelling shut,  
whose sheets smell of surf  
and an absence too large to wash.

I go down where the waves  
break their glass against the reef.  
The cuts on my palms reopen.  
My knee, purple from the rocks,  
speaks in its blunt language.  
Even the body keeps a ledger:  
here he held me,  
here I fell,  
here I would not let go.

Above, frigatebirds tilt like black scissors.  
A bananaquit stitches yellow  
through the hedge. The sea  
pretends to be endless  
because it cannot admit  
what it has taken.

At dusk the Poinciana darkens,  
each blossom closing over its ember.  
I taste blood, then salt, then blood again,  
and watch the last truck vanish  
with its red lights burning.

In the shallows, something silver turns—  
not a fish, only your fishhook,  
rising on the tide  
with a strand of my hair wound tight  
around its barb.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an experimental prose poem that merges Caribbean landscape with trauma and rebirth. Make the imagery lush but unsettling, the punctuation sparse, and the speaker’s body inseparable from the ocean.
counterfactuals.output:
after the hurricane I woke with mangroves  
braided through my ribs  

small red crabs nesting  
where the heart had been loudest  

the sea did not ask permission  
it entered by every blue door in me  
salted the rooms  
lifted the photographs by their pale throats  

all night the palms bent toward the ground  
as if listening for the buried  
as if the buried were singing  

I carried that song in my mouth  
a black pearl  
a storm eye  
a seed slick with blood and rain  

by morning my skin was reef  
bright wounds opening into anemones  
parrotfish grazing the names from my shoulders  

I could no longer tell  
which wave was memory  
which memory had teeth  

beneath me the island steamed  
guava split sweetly in the mud  
breadfruit leaves held bowls of thunder  
and the hills wore green so fierce  
it looked like grief learning to breathe  

I gave the ocean my ruined spine  
it gave me back a current  

I gave it my silence  
it returned a flock of salt birds  

now when I walk  
the tide walks inside me  
pulling moonlight through the marrow  
dragging its nets of bone and hibiscus  

do not call this healing  

call it the drowned body  
growing gills  

call it the wound  
opening its blue mouth  

call it morning  
though the water is still rising
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark feminist poem about a woman navigating desire, danger, and memory on an island, with vivid references to wildlife, red blossoms, broken bones, strangers, and the unforgiving boundaries of the world.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Island Keeps Its Teeth**

At dusk, the island loosens its black hair  
into the sea. I walk beneath it,  
a woman carrying desire like raw meat—  
wrapped badly, dripping through the cloth.

In the mangroves, crocodiles rehearse stillness.  
Fruit bats unhook from the red-blossomed trees,  
their wings opening like burned letters.  
Every flower here has learned the color  
of warning, of birth, of a mouth  
that has bitten through its answer.

Strangers arrive in boats with clean knives,  
calling the shore empty,  
calling my body a country  
because they have brought a flag.

I know this hunger.  
I have seen it polish its boots,  
wash blood from its grammar,  
name fear *permission*  
and silence *peace*.

The jungle keeps my other lives:  
a wrist once broken beneath a lover’s weather,  
a rib cracked white as coral,  
the small bones of trust scattered  
where hermit crabs drag stolen houses  
over the sand.

Memory is not a grave here.  
It breeds. It climbs the walls at night,  
green and muscular,  
lays its eggs beneath my tongue.

Still, I want.  
That is the dangerous miracle—  
not innocence, never that,  
but wanting after the blade,  
after the hand at the throat,  
after the world has drawn its borders  
in salt, law, and men.

Beyond the reef, sharks patrol  
the blue’s hard sentence.  
Behind me, boars root among red petals  
fallen thick as wounds.  
There is nowhere gentle to stand.

So I stand where I am.

I make a torch of the old maps.  
I warm my broken bones above them.  
I let the strangers watch  
as their promised world curls into ash.

The island does not save me.  
It teaches the cost of edges:  
cliff against wave, tooth against skin,  
woman against the unforgiving boundary  
that calls itself natural.

At dawn, I enter the water  
without asking whether it will hold me.

The sea opens its merciless mouth.

I open mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-stanza free-verse poem in an intense, dreamlike style. Begin with “This is where you leave me,” evoke months spent on a white beach, and end on an abrupt image of an owl slipping a hook into the speaker’s cheek.
counterfactuals.output:
This is where you leave me,  
beneath a sky fevered with salt,  
after months spent barefoot on the white beach,  
counting the drowned moons in every shell,  
sleeping where the tide rehearsed my name  
and the palms bent down like burning witnesses.  
All night, your absence wore a silver mask;  
all morning, the sea dragged its blue knives home.  
I opened my mouth to call you back—  
an owl slipped a hook into my cheek.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
